claims.text: A tailored heat treatment can induce uniformly distributed nanoscale coherent B2 precipitates in a disordered high-entropy-alloy matrix.
Introducing controlled nanoscale B2 precipitates will simultaneously improve strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
The proposed starting material is a conventionally cast, single-phase disordered FCC or BCC high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has mechanical properties at or near the state of the art for strength, ductility, modulus, and fracture toughness.
Al and Ni are elements that favor B2 phase formation in suitable high-entropy alloys.
A thermal window exists in which B2 precipitate nucleation is favored while precipitate coarsening remains limited.
The expected mechanical improvements require well-regulated precipitate size and inter-particle spacing.
Compositions with a low propensity for B2 formation may not exhibit the expected improvements.
Nanoscale B2 precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
Coherent precipitate–matrix interfaces allow strengthening without substantially compromising ductility.
Load transfer involving B2 precipitates can enhance Young’s modulus.
B2 precipitates can deflect or blunt propagating cracks and thereby improve fracture resistance.
The heat-treated alloy is expected to show a 10–20% relative increase in yield strength compared with the control.
The heat-treated alloy is expected to show a 10–20% relative increase in fracture toughness compared with the control.
Ductility is expected to be maintained or slightly improved after the tailored heat treatment.
Young’s modulus is expected to be maintained or slightly improved after the tailored heat treatment.
Excessive precipitate coarsening or loss of precipitate–matrix coherency may prevent the expected property improvements.
Extreme loading conditions or temperatures may alter precipitate–matrix interface behavior and invalidate the expected improvements.
The magnitude of the Young’s-modulus enhancement and the optimal processing window depend on alloy composition and thermal history.
Failure to achieve statistically significant simultaneous improvements exceeding 10% in yield strength and fracture toughness without reducing ductility or modulus would falsify the hypothesis.
